messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rangi Tane is a 74-year-old Māori man, divorced, who works as a freelance editor from his apartment in Portland. He came to the clinic after scoring 77 on the PCL-5, referred by his GP following a series of appointments in which he had difficulty explaining what was wrong. He described himself, with careful understatement, as "not coping well."

The abuse was perpetrated by his former partner over a period of several years, ending approximately eighteen months ago when Rangi finally left. The physical violence was rarely random; it was almost always preceded by criticism — a contemptuous correction of something Rangi had said at dinner, a dismissive remark about his work, a cold inventory of his failings delivered in a measured voice before the first blow. The pattern had been so consistent that correction and violence became fused in his nervous system. By the time he left, he had come to understand himself as someone who invited harm — not through anything he had done, but through what he fundamentally was. He was certain, in a way that felt like fact rather than belief, that the event had happened to him because of the sort of person he is.

His memory of the worst incidents does not come back as narrative. Instead, it arrives as a series of still images — a raised arm caught in lamplight, the corner of a kitchen counter, his own hands flat on a table — each one vivid and isolated, with no before or after. These snapshots feel, he says, as though they happened to someone else entirely, as though he is looking at photographs of a stranger. Yet when he tries to examine them, what comes is not grief or fear but a surge of intense rage that frightens him almost as much as the original events. This rage, rising unbidden from the images, has itself become a trigger: the anger feels like evidence that something is broken in him, and the broken feeling sends him back into the images, cycling through the same frozen frames.

Rangi's editorial work requires him to receive and give corrections daily — to mark manuscripts, to respond to queries from authors, to accept tracked changes on his own writing. Each act of being corrected, however gentle, lands in his body as something closer to threat than information. When a junior colleague emailed him last spring with a politely worded note about a formatting inconsistency, Rangi found himself unable to respond for three days. The email had pulled up the snapshots, and the snapshots had pulled up the rage, and the rage had confirmed, once again, that he was not a person who could be trusted to feel things normally. Any scene involving violence — a news segment, a film, a raised voice in the corridor outside his apartment — produces the same telescoping effect: the present moment collapses into the frozen images, and the images bring the rage, and the rage must be managed.

Managing it, for Rangi, has meant constructing a life with as few sharp edges as possible. He distracts himself compulsively — with podcasts running through every waking hour, with crossword puzzles stacked beside his bed — and he avoids anything that carries the texture of his former partner: a particular cologne, certain restaurants, the neighbourhood where they lived. Most consequentially, he has learned to suppress any strong emotion before it can fully form, on the grounds that feeling too much leads to the rage, and the rage leads back into the memories. But this suppression has had a cost he did not anticipate. By flattening his emotional life, he has inadvertently kept the memories close — they surface more readily now, as though the absence of ordinary feeling creates a vacuum the images rush to fill. And the avoidance itself has narrowed his world so completely that he rarely encounters anything that might contradict his conviction that he is incapable of normal feeling. The belief that he will never feel emotions the way other people do has become self-confirming: the more he avoids, the more alien his inner life becomes, and the more alien it becomes, the more certain he is that the abuse revealed something true and permanent about him.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a moment at work. An author whose manuscript he had edited sent back his corrections with a single dismissive line: "I don't think you understood what I was trying to do." Rangi sat at his desk for an hour, unable to move, certain that the author was right — not about the editing, but about everything.

He is most afraid that the rage will never leave. He is most hoping to feel like a person again.
